interest: This file provides a revealing window into the complex triangular diplomacy and clandestine intelligence warfare among the United States, Franco's Spain, and the Axis powers during World War II. It illustrates how the Roosevelt administration strategically publicized intelligence on Japanese espionage operations in Madrid through Archibald MacLeish's Office of Facts and Figures, inciting domestic controversy over wartime electioneering as well as immediate formal protests from the Spanish government. Furthermore, the 1944 intelligence reports derived from Yomiuri correspondent Kuninosuke Matsuo offer rare, candid insight into Axis internal fractures near the end of the European war, documenting Spanish Foreign Minister Lequerica's calculated distancing from Nazi Germany, Japanese Minister Suma's profound defeatism, and the sharp intelligence divergence between Tokyo, Madrid, and pro-Nazi Ambassador Hiroshi Oshima in Berlin.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.20252, spanning 1942 to 1945) documents United States monitoring and diplomatic handling of Japanese military intelligence, espionage, and propaganda activities conducted in and through technically neutral Spain during World War II. The file opens in March 1942 with an informal protest by the Spanish Ambassador over American press reports—sparked by Office of Facts and Figures Director Archibald MacLeish—alleging that the Japanese Embassy in Madrid was operating as an Axis clearinghouse for fifth-column propaganda aimed at undermining the Roosevelt administration and fostering racial and political division in the United States. Subsequent materials, including intelligence despatches from Ambassador Carlton J. H. Hayes in 1944, cross-references, and interagency routing slips, track intelligence obtained from Yomiuri correspondent Kuninosuke Matsuo regarding deteriorating German-Japanese relations, Spanish Foreign Minister Lequerica's distancing from the Germans, Japanese Minister Yakichiro Suma's expectation of Axis defeat, and diplomatic maneuvers in Lisbon and Berlin, alongside earlier reports on Japanese cultural propaganda through Catholic missionaries in the Canary Islands.

subfiles.about: Memorandum recording an informal protest by the Spanish Ambassador against U.S. newspaper reports accusing Madrid of being a center for Japanese intrigue.
subfiles.summary: Avra M. Warren reports to Assistant Secretary Breckinridge Long that the Spanish Ambassador telephoned to protest informally against articles in the New York Times and Washington Times-Herald. The ambassador stated that the characterization of Madrid as a hub for Japanese intrigue was particularly offensive to the Spanish Government in its role protecting Japanese interests. Warren assured the ambassador that he would examine the articles and bring his concerns to Long's attention.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Warren to Long regarding Spanish Ambassador's protest over press reports

subfiles.about: New York Times article reporting on statements by OFF Director Archibald MacLeish concerning Axis broadcasts and Japanese espionage conducted through Madrid.
subfiles.summary: Archibald MacLeish, director of the Office of Facts and Figures, warns that Axis propagandists and fifth columnists are attempting to foment disunity in the United States and alienate Latin American allies. He cites a confidential report disclosing that the Japanese Embassy in Madrid is exploiting neutral Spain to gather intelligence and rumor aimed at overthrowing the Roosevelt administration and stoking racial and social strife. The article also notes German radio broadcasts targeting Puerto Rico to incite local nationalist unrest against Governor Rexford Guy Tugwell.
subfiles.title: Newspaper clipping from The New York Times on Axis propaganda and Japanese activities in Madrid

subfiles.about: Washington Times-Herald report analyzing Archibald MacLeish's announcement of a Tokyo plot operating through Madrid in the context of domestic primary elections.
subfiles.summary: The Washington Times-Herald reports on Office of Facts and Figures Director Archibald MacLeish's disclosure of a Japanese intelligence network centered in the Madrid embassy aimed at weakening or overthrowing the Roosevelt administration. Political observers quoted in the piece interpret the announcement as an opening salvo in upcoming primary elections, arguing that the administration is framing political opposition as beneficial to the enemy. The article details the specific intelligence objectives pursued by Japanese attachés in neutral Spain, focusing on political, racial, and economic fissures.
subfiles.title: Newspaper clipping from Washington Times-Herald on MacLeish's release regarding Japanese plot

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting a telegram concerning plain-Japanese instructions sent to Yomiuri correspondent Matsuo in Madrid requesting American military intelligence.
subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference form indexes Telegram No. 1356 sent by Ambassador Carlton J. H. Hayes from Madrid on April 19, 1944. It references a paraphrase of instructions transmitted in plain Japanese to correspondent Kuninosuke Matsuo requesting information on American military affairs. The original communication is filed under decimal file 862.20200/255.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 1356 from Madrid regarding instructions to Matsuo

subfiles.about: Ambassador Hayes transmits an intelligence report based on statements by Japanese journalist Kuninosuke Matsuo regarding Axis relations and defeatism in Spain.
subfiles.summary: U.S. Ambassador Carlton J. H. Hayes transmits to the Secretary of State a secret report obtained through a trusted local American informant in Madrid. The report recounts statements made by Yomiuri representative Kuninosuke Matsuo regarding strained relations between the Japanese and German embassies, Japanese Minister Suma's conviction that Japan faces defeat, and the impending departure of Japanese personnel from Spain and Portugal. Hayes notes that the Embassy refrained from telegraphing the report because another agency had already done so.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3088 from Hayes forwarding intelligence report on Japanese activities (Air Force copy)

subfiles.about: Confidential report detailing statements by Yomiuri correspondent Matsuo on Japanese despondency, German-Japanese frictions, and Spanish diplomatic realignments.
subfiles.summary: A local American informant reports conversations with Kuninosuke Matsuo, the Madrid correspondent for Yomiuri, via an anti-Nazi German friend. Matsuo stated that Spanish Foreign Minister Lequerica is sidelining German Ambassador Dieckhoff in favor of Japanese Minister Yakichiro Suma, who nonetheless remains deeply depressed and convinced of inevitable Japanese defeat. The report further discloses that Japanese diplomats in Madrid expect Ambassador Hiroshi Oshima in Berlin to commit suicide upon Hitler's defeat, and notes that Japanese officials are evacuating Lisbon to avoid entanglement in German capitulation talks.
subfiles.title: Intelligence report on statements by Matsuo regarding Japanese-German relations and defeatism in Madrid

subfiles.about: State Department duplicate copy of Ambassador Hayes's Despatch No. 3088 forwarding intelligence on Japanese diplomatic and espionage maneuvers in Madrid.
subfiles.summary: This copy of Despatch No. 3088 from Ambassador Carlton J. H. Hayes encloses the September 7, 1944 intelligence report on statements made by Yomiuri correspondent Kuninosuke Matsuo. Hayes explains the Embassy's handling of the intelligence gathered by a local American operative engaged in counter-espionage activities. The despatch covers Axis internal discord, Minister Suma's defeatist outlook, and diplomatic shifts within the Spanish Foreign Ministry.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3088 from Hayes forwarding intelligence report on Japanese activities (Department of State copy)

subfiles.about: Official State Department duplicate copy of the September 7, 1944 intelligence report on Japanese diplomatic gloom and Axis frictions in Madrid.
subfiles.summary: This document is the official Department of State file copy of the secret report recounting Yomiuri correspondent Kuninosuke Matsuo's disclosures to an anti-Nazi German source. Matsuo described Spanish Foreign Minister Lequerica's preference for Japanese Minister Suma over German Ambassador Dieckhoff, while emphasizing Suma's despair over Japan's impending loss of the war. The report also highlights Tokyo's growing reliance on neutral posts in Bern and Stockholm over Ambassador Oshima's blindly pro-Nazi reporting from Berlin, and notes the departure of Japanese personnel from Lisbon.
subfiles.title: Intelligence report on statements by Matsuo regarding Japanese-German relations and defeatism in Madrid (duplicate copy)

subfiles.about: State Department charge slip tracking the checkout of the enclosure to Despatch No. 3088 in October 1945.
subfiles.summary: A standard Department of State charge slip records that the enclosure to Despatch No. 3088 (dated September 14, 1944, from Madrid) under file 894.20252 was charged out on October 18, 1945. The slip was initialed by clerk JS for transfer to CS. It demonstrates postwar administrative tracking and review of wartime Japanese espionage records.
subfiles.title: Charge slip for Despatch No. 3088 enclosure

subfiles.about: State Department transmittal memorandum circulating Ambassador Hayes's Despatch No. 3088 and its enclosure to U.S. military and civilian intelligence agencies.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State formally transmits copies of Ambassador Carlton J. H. Hayes's secret Despatch No. 3088 from Madrid to major wartime intelligence and security organizations. The recipients listed are the Military Intelligence Service (MIS), the Office of Naval Intelligence (ONI), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and the Office of Strategic Services (OSS). The routing reflects the interagency distribution and intelligence value attached to Matsuo's reports on Japanese and German activities.
subfiles.title: Department of State transmission sheet distributing Despatch No. 3088 to intelligence agencies
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Service, Office of Naval Intelligence, Federal Bureau of Investigation, Office of Strategic Services

subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum reporting that a Catholic missionary priest was touring Spain exhibiting films provided by the Japanese Foreign Ministry.
subfiles.summary: Herbert Fales of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs informs Laurence E. Salisbury of an item from Las Palmas Despatch No. 11, dated February 19, 1942. According to a Canary Islands newspaper, a Catholic missionary priest touring Spain had received fifty films from the Japanese Foreign Ministry to raise funds before returning to Japan. While the U.S. Consul noted the priest's ostensible purpose was religious, he warned that the screenings offered an opportunity for Japanese propaganda dissemination.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Fales on Japanese film propaganda by a Catholic missionary in Spain
